drills.q: A teammate says 'our new model has higher AUC-ROC, so it's strictly better.' What's the specific scenario where this is wrong?
drills.a: AUC-ROC aggregates across all thresholds, but production operates at one specific threshold. A model can win on average AUC-ROC while performing worse at the actual operating region that matters (e.g. low-FPR region relevant to a fraud alert budget) -- compare precision-recall curves at the real deployment operating point, not the aggregate area.

drills.q: On a dataset with 1,000 positives and 99,000 negatives, a model catches 800 true positives with 2,000 false positives. Compute FPR and precision and explain why they tell different stories.
drills.a: FPR = 2000/99000 ~ 2.0% (looks great, keeps AUC-ROC high). Precision = 800/(800+2000) ~ 28.6% (more than 70% of flagged items are false alarms). FPR is normalized against the huge negative class, hiding the false-alarm burden that precision reveals.

drills.q: You have 200 calibration examples with a 5% positive rate. Would you use Platt scaling or isotonic regression, and why?
drills.a: Platt scaling -- with only ~10 positive examples, isotonic regression's flexible many-parameter step function would almost certainly overfit badly in the sparse positive region, while Platt's two-parameter sigmoid fit is far more robust to limited data, even though it assumes a specific shape.

drills.q: A fraud model has false-negative cost $500 and false-positive cost $15. Derive the cost-minimizing probability threshold, and state what must be true of the model for this derivation to be valid.
drills.a: Flag as fraud when p*500 > (1-p)*15, giving threshold p* = 15/515 ~ 2.9%. This derivation requires the model's probabilities to be genuinely calibrated -- if p is miscalibrated (e.g. systematically overconfident), the derived cutoff is applied to the wrong underlying probabilities and won't actually minimize expected cost.

drills.q: A model's accuracy and AUC-ROC dashboards look stable in production, but a teammate suspects calibration has quietly degraded. What monitoring would catch this, and why wouldn't accuracy/AUC show it?
drills.a: Track a reliability diagram or ECE on a rolling window of production data with ground truth, watching for drift away from the diagonal. If the underlying base rate shifts while relative ranking of risk stays intact, AUC-ROC (rank-based) and accuracy (if the threshold still roughly separates classes) can look stable even though every predicted probability is now systematically wrong relative to the new true rate.

drills.q: Why is it wrong to calibrate a model on the same data it was trained on, and does this same concern extend to your final evaluation set?
drills.a: A model's scores on its own training data are systematically overconfident (partial memorization), so a calibration mapping fit there matches that overconfidence, not true out-of-sample behavior. Yes, the same leakage risk applies if the calibration set is also your final evaluation set -- reported calibration quality (ECE, reliability diagram) would be optimistically biased toward that data. Use three splits when sample size allows: train base model, calibrate, final-evaluate.

drills.q: Explain why isotonic regression's calibrated output is a step function rather than a smooth curve, and when that's actually a problem.
drills.a: Pool-adjacent-violators merges adjacent blocks violating monotonicity and assigns each merged block's average as the calibrated value for every point in it -- producing a non-decreasing step function with jumps at block boundaries, not a smooth curve. This is a problem when a smooth estimate is needed downstream (e.g. feeding a gradient-based optimization) or when a boundary falls in an operationally important, sparsely-populated region, producing an abrupt, poorly-estimated jump exactly where precision matters most.

drills.q: A stakeholder is impressed by an AUC-PR of 0.3 on one project and unimpressed by the same 0.3 on another. Could both reactions be correct?
drills.a: Yes -- a random classifier's AUC-PR equals the positive class prevalence, not a fixed baseline like AUC-ROC's 0.5. An AUC-PR of 0.3 on a 1%-prevalence dataset is a large lift over the 0.01 random baseline; the same 0.3 on a 30%-prevalence dataset is barely above random baseline. AUC-PR values are not comparable across datasets without accounting for base rate.
